newsitem.title: USA: A.H. Belo to buy Providence Journal for $1.5 bln.
newsitem.headline: A.H. Belo to buy Providence Journal for $1.5 bln.

text.p: A.H. Belo Corp. said Thursday it agreed to buy newspaper and television company The Providence Journal Co. in a $1.5 billion cash-and-stock deal forming one of the largest U.S. media companies.

Dallas-based Belo, which publishes the Dallas Morning News, would acquire the Providence Journal-Bulletin, the leading paper in Rhode Island and southeastern Massachusetts, as well as a slew of television stations around the country.

The deal will make Belo the nation's eighth largest television group measured by revenues and the 10th largest in audience reach with the addition of Providence Journal's nine owned-and-operated TV stations, including five NBC affiliates and affiliates of ABC, CBS and Fox.
Belo currently owns seven network-affiliated stations: three CBS, three ABC and one affiliate of the new UPN network.
They give Belo access to eight percent of U.S. households but that will rise to 12.3 percent once the acquisition is completed following approval from federal regulators.
Belo and Providence Journal had combined revenues of $1.1 billion for the 12 months ended June 30, 1996.
"This combination of broadcast assets creates one of the finest network-affiliated station groups in the country," Belo Chairman Robert Decherd said in a statement.
Belo executives said they were determined to jump on the buy-out bandwagon which is running through the broadcast industry rather than get left behind.

"The industry is consolidating and in order to achieve the economies of scale that are available, and perhaps even to stay in the business, one needs to consolidate along with it," Chief Financial Officer Michael Perry said in an interview.
He said Belo had been interested in strategic broadcast growth for several years and that a hefty stock offer earlier this year strengthened its balance sheet ahead of the acquisition.
He also said Belo is looking out for further targets. "The company still has a pretty strong balance sheet and has capacity for further acquisitions."

Belo's current broadcast stations include WFAA-TV in Dallas, KHOU-TV in Houston, WWL-TV in New Orleans and KOTV in Tulsa, Okla. Providence Journal's stations include KING-TV in Seattle, KGW-TV in Portland, Ore., KHNL-TV in Honolulu and KMSB-TV in Tucson, Ariz.

Perry said that, of all Providence Journal's stations, KING-TV in Seattle, an NBC affiliate, was "the one that is really of interest to us" because of the city's strong demographics and growth profile.

Providence, R.I.-based Providence Journal's cable TV businesses include a 46 percent stake in the Television Food Network and a 65 percent stake in America's Health Network. It also owns NorthWest Cable News, a regional cable channel in the Pacific Northwest.

"In this consolidating environment, The Providence Journal Co. could not find a better partner with whom to entrust its people and franchises to than Belo," said Providence Journal Chairman Stephen Hamblett.
Under the deal Providence Journal shareholders would receive $12.33 in cash and 0.5333 shares of Belo series A common stock for each share of Providence Journal.
Providence Journal will become a wholly-owned subsidiary of Belo, and four directors from Providence Journal will join Belo's board, the companies said.
The deal would increase the number of Belo's total shares outstanding from 44.3 million to 69.7 million and the payment of $587 million in cash to Providence Journal holders, the companies said.
Belo also publishes the Owensboro (Ky.) Messenger-Inquirer, The Bryan-College Station (Texas) Eagle and the Arlington (Texas) Morning News.
Perry said the merger would give Belo greater bargaining power to buy news print and broadcast programming at cheaper rates.
He said the deal must still be approved by the Federal Communications Commission to transfer station licenses but that it should be completed in the first half of 1997.
